entries.lesson_core_move: Express a periodic continuous-time signal in complex-exponential Fourier series form as a sum of integer-harmonic terms C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t} with each coefficient weighting one harmonic.

sections.section_title: Writing a Periodic Signal as a Complex Harmonic Sum

prompt_blocks.text: Given the explicit harmonic terms $C_{-2}e^{-j2\omega_0 t}$, $C_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0 t}$, $C_0$, $C_1e^{j\omega_0 t}$, and $C_2e^{j2\omega_0 t}$, which compact form matches this periodic signal?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The finite list already shows the DC term and the positive/negative harmonic pairs. The compact Fourier-series form writes the same pattern as one sum over all integers, with one coefficient per harmonic.
So the correct compact form is $x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given the explicit harmonic terms $C_3e^{j3\omega_0 t}$, $C_2e^{j2\omega_0 t}$, $C_1e^{j\omega_0 t}$, $C_0$, $C_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0 t}$, $C_{-2}e^{-j2\omega_0 t}$, and $C_{-3}e^{-j3\omega_0 t}$, which compact form matches this periodic signal?

choice_blocks.text: $x(t)=C_{-3}e^{-j3\omega_0 t}+C_{-2}e^{-j2\omega_0 t}+C_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0 t}+C_0+C_1e^{j\omega_0 t}+C_2e^{j2\omega_0 t}+C_3e^{j3\omega_0 t}$
$x(t)=C_{-3}e^{-j3\omega_0 t}+C_{-2}e^{-j2\omega_0 t}+C_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0 t}+C_1e^{j\omega_0 t}+C_2e^{j2\omega_0 t}+C_3e^{j3\omega_0 t}$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The order of the finite list does not matter. The DC term is still the $k=0$ coefficient, and the full compact form is the same sum over all integer harmonics.
So the correct compact form is $x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$.

sections.section_title: Substituting the Fundamental Frequency into the Series Form

prompt_blocks.text: For a periodic signal with period $T_0=6$, which series expression is obtained after substituting the fundamental frequency into $x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The period $T_0=6$ gives $\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{T_0}=\frac{2\pi}{6}=\frac{\pi}{3}$. Substituting that value into every $\omega_0$ in the series gives $x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k e^{jk(\pi/3)t}$, while leaving the coefficient pattern and integer index range unchanged.

prompt_blocks.text: For a periodic signal with fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0=\pi/4$, which series expression is obtained after substituting into $x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because the fundamental angular frequency is already given as $\omega_0=\pi/4$, the substitution is direct: replace each $\omega_0$ in the series with $\pi/4$ and keep the coefficients and integer index range the same. That gives $x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} C_k e^{jk(\pi/4)t}$.

sections.section_title: Expanding the Sum into Indexed Harmonic Terms

prompt_blocks.text: Expand $\sum_{k=-1}^{1} A_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$ into explicit harmonic terms.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The bounds run from $k=-1$ to $k=1$, so the explicit expansion has three terms: the negative harmonic, the $k=0$ DC term, and the positive harmonic in order.

prompt_blocks.text: Expand $\sum_{k=-3}^{3} B_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$ into explicit harmonic terms.

choice_blocks.text: $B_{-3}e^{-j3\omega_0 t}+B_{-2}e^{-j2\omega_0 t}+B_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0 t}+B_0+B_1e^{j\omega_0 t}+B_2e^{j2\omega_0 t}+B_3e^{j3\omega_0 t}$
$B_3e^{j3\omega_0 t}+B_2e^{j2\omega_0 t}+B_1e^{j\omega_0 t}+B_0+B_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0 t}+B_{-2}e^{-j2\omega_0 t}+B_{-3}e^{-j3\omega_0 t}$
$B_{-3}e^{-j3\omega_0 t}+B_{-2}e^{-j2\omega_0 t}+B_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0 t}+B_1e^{j\omega_0 t}+B_2e^{j2\omega_0 t}+B_3e^{j3\omega_0 t}$

questions.correct_answer: $B_{-3}e^{-j3\omega_0 t}+B_{-2}e^{-j2\omega_0 t}+B_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0 t}+B_0+B_1e^{j\omega_0 t}+B_2e^{j2\omega_0 t}+B_3e^{j3\omega_0 t}$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The bounds run from $k=-3$ to $k=3$, so you list the negative harmonics first, include the $k=0$ term, and then write the positive harmonics in order.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Coefficient Weight on a Harmonic Term

prompt_blocks.text: Given the term $C_3 e^{j3\omega_0 t}$, which coefficient weights that harmonic?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the harmonic index from the exponential term: $e^{j3\omega_0 t}$ means $k=3$. The matching coefficient label is therefore $C_3$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given the term $C_{-4} e^{-j4\omega_0 t}$, which coefficient weights that harmonic?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The exponential $e^{-j4\omega_0 t}$ shows harmonic index $k=-4$. The coefficient that weights that term has the same index and sign, so the answer is $C_{-4}$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret each complex Fourier coefficient C_k as the magnitude-and-phase weight assigned to the kth complex-exponential harmonic in a periodic signal.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Harmonic Indexed by a Coefficient

prompt_blocks.text: In the term $C_{-2}e^{-j2\omega_0 t}$, which harmonic does $C_{-2}$ weight?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The subscript is $-2$, so $C_{-2}$ weights the $-2$nd harmonic. The exponential matches that same index, but the harmonic number comes from the subscript.

prompt_blocks.text: In the term $C_4e^{j4\omega_0 t}$, which harmonic does $C_4$ weight?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The subscript is $4$, so $C_4$ weights the $4$th harmonic. The exponent matches that same index, but the harmonic label comes from the coefficient subscript.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Coefficient Magnitude as Harmonic Weight

prompt_blocks.text: If $C_4 = 6e^{-j\pi/5}$, what is the weight of the 4th harmonic?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The weight is the magnitude of the coefficient. For $C_4 = 6e^{-j\pi/5}$, the magnitude is $|C_4| = 6$, and the phase does not change the harmonic weight.

prompt_blocks.text: If $C_{-3} = \frac{1}{2}e^{j2\pi/3}$, what is the weight of the $-3$rd harmonic?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The weight is the magnitude of the coefficient, so $|C_{-3}| = \frac{1}{2}$. The phase $2\pi/3$ and the index $-3$ are separate from the harmonic weight.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Coefficient Phase as Harmonic Phase

prompt_blocks.text: If $C_1=2e^{-j\pi/6}$, what phase does the 1st harmonic carry?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The phase is the angle in the polar form, so read $-\pi/6$ from the exponential. The magnitude $2$ tells you the harmonic's strength, but it does not change the phase.

prompt_blocks.text: If $C_{-2}=5e^{j\pi/3}$, what phase does the $-2$nd harmonic carry?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The phase is the angle in the exponential, so read $\pi/3$ from the coefficient. The magnitude $5$ and the harmonic index $-2$ are separate pieces of information.

sections.section_title: Reading Nonzero Coefficients as Present Harmonics

prompt_blocks.text: Which harmonics are present if $C_{-2}=0$, $C_{-1}=1+j$, $C_0=0$, $C_1=2e^{-j\pi/3}$, and $C_2=0$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A harmonic is present exactly when its coefficient is nonzero. Here only $C_{-1}$ and $C_1$ are nonzero, so the $-1$st and $1$st harmonics are present.

prompt_blocks.text: Which harmonics are present if $C_{-2}=3e^{-j\pi/6}$, $C_{-1}=0$, $C_0=4$, $C_1=0$, and $C_2=5e^{j\pi/4}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A harmonic is present exactly when its coefficient is nonzero. Here $C_{-2}$, $C_0$, and $C_2$ are nonzero, so the $-2$nd harmonic, the DC term at $k=0$, and the $2$nd harmonic are present.

entries.lesson_core_move: Evaluate complex Fourier coefficients by integrating x(t)e^{-jk\omega_0 t} over any one period and normalizing by the period to isolate the kth harmonic.

sections.section_title: Identifying T_0, omega_0, and k in the Coefficient Formula

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal has $T_0=4$. Which coefficient formula correctly sets up $C_2$ over the one-period interval $[1,5]$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The interval $[1,5]$ has length $4$, so $T_0=4$ and $\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}$. With $k=2$, the kernel is $e^{-j2\omega_0 t}=e^{-j\pi t}$.

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal has $T_0=6$. Which coefficient formula correctly sets up $C_4$ over the one-period interval $[-3,3]$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The interval $[-3,3]$ has length $6$, so $T_0=6$ and $\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{6}=\frac{\pi}{3}$. With $k=4$, the kernel is $e^{-j4\omega_0 t}=e^{-j\frac{4\pi}{3}t}$.

sections.section_title: Computing C_k from a Smooth Periodic Formula

prompt_blocks.text: What is $C_1$ for $x(t)=2+3\cos(\pi t)-4\sin(2\pi t)$ over one period?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The period is $T_0=2$, so $\omega_0=\pi$. For $k=1$, the matching harmonic comes from the $3\cos(\pi t)$ term.
So the coefficient on $e^{j\pi t}$ is $C_1=\frac{3}{2}$. The DC term and the $2\pi$ sine term do not contribute to $k=1$.

prompt_blocks.text: What is $C_2$ for $x(t)=1+5\cos(2\pi t)+4\sin(2\pi t)$ over one period?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $k=2$, only the $2\pi$ harmonic matters. Expand the matching cosine and sine terms and read off the coefficient of $e^{j2\pi t}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.latex: 5\cos(2\pi t)+4\sin(2\pi t)=\frac{5}{2}\bigl(e^{j2\pi t}+e^{-j2\pi t}\bigr)-2j\bigl(e^{j2\pi t}-e^{-j2\pi t}\bigr)

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The $e^{j2\pi t}$ coefficient is $\frac{5}{2}-2j$, and the DC term does not contribute to $C_2$.

sections.section_title: Computing C_k Over a Shifted One-Period Interval

prompt_blocks.text: For the same signal as in the example, what is $C_2$ if the integral is taken over $[1,3]$ instead of $[0,2]$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The coefficient integrand is $2$-periodic, so any interval of length $2$ gives the same average. Shifting the window from $[0,2]$ to $[1,3]$ does not change the coefficient, so the answer is $2j$.

prompt_blocks.text: For the same signal as in the example, what is $C_2$ if the integral is taken over $[-1,1]$ instead of $[0,2]$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The interval $[-1,1]$ still has length $2$, so it is one full period. Because the coefficient integrand is periodic with that same period, the shifted window gives the same coefficient: $C_2=2j$.

sections.section_title: Splitting the Coefficient Integral Across Pieces of One Period

prompt_blocks.text: What is $C_1$ for the periodic signal $x(t)=1$ on $0\le t<\frac{1}{2}$ and $x(t)=3$ on $\frac{1}{2}\le t<2$, with $T_0=2$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Split the integral at the change point $t=\frac{1}{2}$, evaluate each piece, and then apply the $\frac{1}{2}$ normalization.
The coefficient is $\frac{-1+j}{\pi}$.

prompt_blocks.text: What is $C_{-1}$ for the same periodic signal $x(t)=1$ on $0\le t<\frac{1}{2}$ and $x(t)=3$ on $\frac{1}{2}\le t<2$, with $T_0=2$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the same split, but for $k=-1$ the exponential is $e^{j\pi t}$ instead of $e^{-j\pi t}$.
So the coefficient is $\frac{-1-j}{\pi}$.

sections.section_title: Checking That the Integral Isolates the kth Harmonic

prompt_blocks.text: By direct integration over one period, what is $C_{-1}$ for $x(t)=3+4e^{-j\pi t}+9e^{j4\pi t}$ with $T_0=2$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The matching harmonic is the $k=-1$ term, so the integral isolates the coefficient on $e^{-j\pi t}$. The DC term and the $k=4$ term are nonmatching, so they integrate to zero over one period. That leaves $C_{-1}=4$.

prompt_blocks.text: By direct integration over one period, what is $C_{3}$ for $x(t)=6-5e^{j3\pi t}+2e^{-j\pi t}$ with $T_0=2$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The matching harmonic is the $k=3$ term, so the coefficient integral isolates the term $-5e^{j3\pi t}$. The DC term and the $k=-1$ term are nonmatching and vanish over one period. Therefore $C_3=-5$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the DC coefficient C_0 by setting k=0 in the complex Fourier coefficient integral and interpreting the result as the periodic signal's average value.

sections.section_title: Computing C_0 by Setting k=0 in the Coefficient Integral

prompt_blocks.text: Compute $C_0$ for the periodic signal that equals $6$ on $0 \le t < T_0/4$ and $2$ on $T_0/4 \le t < T_0$ by setting $k=0$ in the coefficient integral.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set $k=0$, so the exponential factor becomes $1$ and $C_0$ is the one-period average.
That gives $\frac{1}{T_0}\left(6\frac{T_0}{4} + 2\frac{3T_0}{4}\right) = 3$, so the correct choice is $A$.

prompt_blocks.text: Compute $C_0$ for the periodic signal that equals $8$ on $0 \le t < T_0/3$ and $2$ on $T_0/3 \le t < T_0$ by setting $k=0$ in the coefficient integral.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Again set $k=0$, so the exponential factor becomes $1$ and the coefficient is the one-period average.
That gives $\frac{1}{T_0}\left(8\frac{T_0}{3} + 2\frac{2T_0}{3}\right) = 4$, so the correct choice is $A$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting C_0 as the Average Value Over One Period

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal equals $6$ on $0 \le t < T_0/3$, $0$ on $T_0/3 \le t < 2T_0/3$, and $2$ on $2T_0/3 \le t < T_0$. What is the signal's average value, and therefore $C_0$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because the three subintervals all have the same length, the average is the simple average of the three levels. The zero section contributes no area, but it still counts in the one-period average.
So the signal's average value is $\frac{8}{3}$, so the correct choice is $A$.

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal equals $5$ on $0 \le t < T_0/4$ and $-1$ on $T_0/4 \le t < T_0$. What is the signal's average value, and therefore $C_0$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the weighted one-period average: the short positive piece contributes $5\cdot \frac{1}{4}$, while the long negative piece contributes $-1\cdot \frac{3}{4}$. Because the positive area is larger, the mean stays above zero.
So the average value is $\frac{1}{2}$, so the correct choice is $A$.

sections.section_title: Choosing a Convenient Period for Computing C_0

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal with period $T_0=4$ is defined by $x(t)=2$ on $1 \le t < 3$ and $x(t)=6$ on $3 \le t < 5$, repeated periodically. Compute $C_0$ by integrating over the convenient one-period interval $[1,5]$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The interval $[1,5]$ is one full period and it lines up with the breakpoint at $t=3$, so no extra splitting is needed. The two pieces each have length 2, so the total area is 16, and dividing by $T_0=4$ gives $C_0=4$.

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal with period $T_0=4$ is defined by $x(t)=5$ on $-1 \le t < 1$ and $x(t)=1$ on $1 \le t < 3$, repeated periodically. Compute $C_0$ by integrating over the convenient one-period interval $[-1,3]$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The interval $[-1,3]$ is one full period and already matches the break at $t=1$. The two pieces each have length 2, so the total area is 12, and dividing by $T_0=4$ gives $C_0=3$.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Zero and Nonzero DC Coefficients from Signal Balance

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal equals $2$ on $0 \le t < T_0/3$ and $-1$ on $T_0/3 \le t < T_0$. Determine whether $C_0$ is zero or nonzero and compute its value from the balance of positive and negative area.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The positive area is $2(T_0/3)=2T_0/3$ and the negative area is $-1(2T_0/3)=-2T_0/3$, so the net signed area is $0$. Dividing by $T_0$ gives $C_0=0$.

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal equals $1$ on $0 \le t < T_0/4$ and $-1$ on $T_0/4 \le t < T_0$. Determine whether $C_0$ is zero or nonzero and compute its value from the balance of positive and negative area.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The positive area is $1(T_0/4)=T_0/4$ and the negative area is $-1(3T_0/4)=-3T_0/4$, so the net signed area is $-T_0/2$. Dividing by $T_0$ gives $C_0=-1/2$.

entries.lesson_title: Relationship Between Trigonometric and Complex Forms
entries.lesson_core_move: Convert between trigonometric and complex Fourier series forms by mapping the DC term and each sine-cosine harmonic pair to the corresponding positive- and negative-index complex coefficients.

sections.lesson_title: Relationship Between Trigonometric and Complex Forms
sections.section_title: Mapping the DC Term Between Fourier Series Forms

prompt_blocks.text: If a trigonometric Fourier series has $a_0=14$, what is the corresponding complex DC coefficient $C_0$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For the DC term, the mapping is $C_0=\frac{a_0}{2}$. The prompt gives $a_0=14$, so $C_0=\frac{14}{2}=7$.

prompt_blocks.text: If a complex Fourier series has $C_0=7$, what is the corresponding trigonometric DC term $a_0$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The reverse DC mapping is $a_0=2C_0$. Substituting $C_0=7$ gives $a_0=2\cdot 7=14$.

sections.lesson_title: Relationship Between Trigonometric and Complex Forms
sections.section_title: Converting a Cosine Harmonic to Complex Coefficients

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=10\cos(2\omega_0 t)$, which pair $(C_2,C_{-2})$ matches the complex form?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A cosine harmonic splits evenly between the positive- and negative-index exponentials. Divide the amplitude by $2$ to get the pair of real coefficients.
So $C_2=5$ and $C_{-2}=5$. The other choices either miss the $1/2$ split, flip the signs, or add imaginary parts that a cosine harmonic does not have.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=14\cos(5\omega_0 t)$, which pair $(C_5,C_{-5})$ matches the complex form?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: This is the same cosine-only split as the worked example, just with a different amplitude and harmonic index. Divide $14$ by $2$ and keep the coefficients real and equal.
So $C_5=7$ and $C_{-5}=7$. The distractors either skip the $1/2$ split, halve twice, flip the sign, or use the wrong harmonic index.

sections.lesson_title: Relationship Between Trigonometric and Complex Forms
sections.section_title: Converting a Sine Harmonic to Complex Coefficients

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=10\sin(4\omega_0 t)$, which pair $(C_4,C_{-4})$ matches the complex form?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the sine identity. A pure sine harmonic gives a purely imaginary conjugate pair with opposite signs.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=8\sin(3\omega_0 t)$, which pair $(C_3,C_{-3})$ matches the complex form?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the same sine identity. The only change is the amplitude and harmonic index, so the coefficients stay imaginary with opposite signs.

sections.lesson_title: Relationship Between Trigonometric and Complex Forms
sections.section_title: Converting a Sine-Cosine Harmonic Pair to Complex Coefficients

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=6\cos(4\omega_0 t)-8\sin(4\omega_0 t)$, which pair $(C_4, C_{-4})$ matches the complex form?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the mixed-pair rule: for $a\cos(k\omega_0 t)+b\sin(k\omega_0 t)$, $C_k=\frac{1}{2}(a-jb)$ and $C_{-k}=\frac{1}{2}(a+jb)$.
So the correct pair is $(C_4, C_{-4})=(3+4j, 3-4j)$. The cosine part contributes the shared real value, and the sine sign determines the opposite imaginary parts.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=10\cos(4\omega_0 t)+6\sin(4\omega_0 t)$, which pair $(C_4, C_{-4})$ matches the complex form?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the same mixed-pair rule with $a=10$ and $b=6$. The cosine term gives the shared real part, and the sine term gives opposite imaginary parts.
So the correct pair is $(C_4, C_{-4})=(5-3j, 5+3j)$. This is the same conversion as the example, with the sign on the sine term reversed.

sections.lesson_title: Relationship Between Trigonometric and Complex Forms
sections.section_title: Converting Complex Coefficient Pairs Back to Sine and Cosine Coefficients

prompt_blocks.text: If $C_3=2-j$ and $C_{-3}=2+j$, which trigonometric coefficient pair $(a_3,b_3)$ is correct?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the reverse mapping on the conjugate pair: add the coefficients to get $a_3$, and subtract them, then multiply by $j$, to get $b_3$.
So the correct trigonometric coefficient pair is $(4, 2)$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $C_4=3+2j$ and $C_{-4}=3-2j$, which trigonometric coefficient pair $(a_4,b_4)$ is correct?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The same reverse formulas apply. The sum gives $a_4$, and the difference times $j$ gives $b_4$.
So the correct trigonometric coefficient pair is $(6, -4)$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret positive and negative harmonics as paired complex exponentials whose coefficients combine to represent each nonzero harmonic of a periodic signal.

sections.section_title: Identifying Positive and Negative Harmonic Indices

prompt_blocks.text: What signed harmonic index is attached to the term $C_{-3}e^{-j3\omega_0 t}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The subscript on the term is $-3$, so the signed harmonic index is $-3$. The negative sign on the index makes it a negative harmonic.

prompt_blocks.text: What signed harmonic index is attached to the term $C_4e^{j4\omega_0 t}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The subscript on the term is $+4$, so the signed harmonic index is $+4$. The positive sign on the index makes it a positive harmonic.

sections.section_title: Matching the Positive and Negative Terms for the Same Harmonic

prompt_blocks.text: Which term is the negative counterpart of $C_4e^{j4\omega_0 t}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The negative counterpart keeps the same harmonic magnitude and flips the sign of the harmonic index. So $C_4e^{j4\omega_0 t}$ matches with $C_{-4}e^{-j4\omega_0 t}$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which pair correctly matches the positive and negative terms for harmonic number $3$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A matched harmonic pair uses the same absolute harmonic index with opposite signs. The $+3$ term therefore pairs with the $-3$ term, so choice A is the only correct pair.

sections.section_title: Interpreting a Harmonic Pair as One Nonzero Frequency Component

prompt_blocks.text: Which statement correctly interprets the pair $C_5e^{j5\omega_0 t}+C_{-5}e^{-j5\omega_0 t}$ as one nonzero harmonic component?

choice_blocks.text: It is one nonzero harmonic component with harmonic number $5$, so its frequency magnitude is $5\omega_0$.
It is two separate harmonics, one at $5\omega_0$ and one at $-5\omega_0$, so the pair should be split apart.
It is the DC component because positive and negative indices always cancel.
It is the $C_5$ coefficient by itself, and the $C_{-5}$ term is a separate harmonic.
It is one nonzero harmonic component with harmonic number $10$, so its frequency magnitude is $10\omega_0$.

questions.correct_answer: It is one nonzero harmonic component with harmonic number $5$, so its frequency magnitude is $5\omega_0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The $+5$ and $-5$ terms form one matched harmonic pair. That means they describe a single nonzero component at harmonic number $5$, with frequency magnitude $5\omega_0$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which statement correctly interprets the pair $C_{-3}e^{-j3\omega_0 t}+C_3e^{j3\omega_0 t}$ as one nonzero harmonic component?

choice_blocks.text: It is one nonzero harmonic component with harmonic number $3$, so its frequency magnitude is $3\omega_0$.
It is two separate harmonics because the negative-index term comes first.
It is the DC component because the terms are written in opposite order.
It is the $C_{-3}$ coefficient by itself, and the $C_3$ term is only a duplicate.
It is one nonzero harmonic component with harmonic number $4$, so its frequency magnitude is $4\omega_0$.

questions.correct_answer: It is one nonzero harmonic component with harmonic number $3$, so its frequency magnitude is $3\omega_0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The $\pm 3$ terms are one matched harmonic pair, even though they are written in reverse order. Together they represent one nonzero component at harmonic number $3$, with frequency magnitude $3\omega_0$.

sections.section_title: Separating Nonzero Harmonic Pairs from the DC Term

prompt_blocks.text: Separate the DC term from the nonzero harmonic pairs in the series below.

prompt_blocks.latex: x(t)=C_4e^{j4\omega_0 t}+C_{-4}e^{-j4\omega_0 t}+C_0+C_1e^{j\omega_0 t}+C_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0 t}+C_3e^{j3\omega_0 t}+C_{-3}e^{-j3\omega_0 t}

choice_blocks.text: $C_0+\big(C_1e^{j\omega_0 t}+C_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0 t}\big)+\big(C_3e^{j3\omega_0 t}+C_{-3}e^{-j3\omega_0 t}\big)+\big(C_4e^{j4\omega_0 t}+C_{-4}e^{-j4\omega_0 t}\big)$
$(C_0+C_1e^{j\omega_0 t})+\big(C_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0 t}+C_3e^{j3\omega_0 t}\big)+\big(C_{-3}e^{-j3\omega_0 t}+C_4e^{j4\omega_0 t}\big)+C_{-4}e^{-j4\omega_0 t}$
